data.claim: Yes: services/ask verdict() trusts the folded log, so a hand-appended ask.answered with human=true is an approved verdict, even for an ask that was minted with a one-time code (coded is self-reported). Only the engine's answer() refuses agents.

chunk_findings.detail: The recommended default in Q6 allows T3 actions (approval config, roles, signers, forbidden-commands, key rotation) to be satisfied by L1 terminal "when no signer is configured". However, D-RA-3 explicitly states that a same-uid agent can forge L1-L3 by editing files. With no signer configured, a malicious or compromised same-uid agent can forge an L1 terminal approval and execute any T3 action, e.g., add an attacker-controlled signer or rotate keys, permanently compromising the approval system. This bootstrap hole makes the proposed default unsafe and defeats the control the design is intended to provide.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md Q6 (and D-RA-3)

chunk_findings.detail: The design is internally contradictory about Class B relayed consent. §4.3 says the old `--yes --reason` flags “keep working until a tier says otherwise (section 7),” but §7 makes T2 per-instance approval “the default for every operator act in family A and B,” including `upgrade --self`, `plan confirm`, and skew override. Under the document’s own default, the tier does say otherwise immediately. If §7 is implemented as written, an `upgrade --self --yes --reason` call must be refused, so §4.3’s compatibility statement is false. If §4.3 is taken as true and those flags remain accepted by default, a prompt-injected instruction can make the agent self-authorize with an invented reason, contradicting the stated goal of “no forgery by classes 1 and 2, by construction.”
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §4.3 vs §7

chunk_findings.detail: The proposal adds `ddflow_session ask` with `wait_s`, which “blocks on elicitation when the client supports it.” This is a direct hold while waiting for operator approval and violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which states agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting. Example: an agent invoking this action blocks inside the tool call until the operator answers or a timeout fires, creating the exact stall the rule forbids.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §10 `ddflow_session ask ... wait_s`

chunk_findings.detail: §4.2 claims that carrying proof and re-verifying it in `verdict` “closes Finding 1 for levels L2 and above.” But §5 defines L2 harness attestation as verified only “as far as the client’s integrity” and its own channel table says a same-uid agent can forge L2 by an auto-accept hook or by editing the hook/transcript record. In that environment the agent can produce a passing L2 proof and append the corresponding `ask.answered` line; re-verifying that forged proof still succeeds, so Finding 1 is not closed for L2. The closure claim requires an unreachable writer/client, which the proposal neither requires nor verifies.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §4.2 vs §5

chunk_findings.detail: The revised Q6 still leaves the bootstrap compromise from the prior finding intact. D-RA-3 establishes that a same-uid agent can forge L1-L3 by editing files. With the empty signer state, the new rule accepts L1 "only to enroll the first signer," but that is itself a T3 signer-configuration action. A malicious same-uid agent can forge an L1 terminal approval and enroll its own public key as that first signer. Once a signer exists, later T3 actions require L4, but the attacker now controls the signing key and can sign arbitrary T3 requests (rotation, roles, forbidden-commands). The doctor flag "T3 protected only by L1 until done" is post hoc and does not block the enrollment or later signed actions, so the same compromise remains; the new wording only narrows the escape hatch to the one forgeable action that is sufficient to bootstrap trust.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md Q6 table row

chunk_findings.detail: The fix still permits the exact bootstrap takeover from the original finding. With no signer configured, a T3 act “can be answered at L1 only to enroll the first signer.” But D-RA-3 and this same doc state a same-uid agent can forge L1 by editing files, so an attacker can forge an L1 terminal answer and enroll its own signer key while no signer exists. From then on it controls the signer and can produce the L4 signatures required for every later T3 act. The new `doctor` warning does not block this, and §4.2’s assertion that L4 is “a signature the agent cannot make” is false along this path. The original high-severity issue remains.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §7 T3 bullet

chunk_findings.detail: This delta does not modify §10. The proposal still adds `ddflow_session ask` with `wait_s`, which blocks on elicitation while the caller waits for operator approval or a timeout. That is a direct hold while waiting and violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting. The triage claimed this was fixed in commit d3e7bb16b, but the shown diff leaves the blocking hold in place, so the finding still holds.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §10 `ddflow_session ask ... wait_s`

chunk_findings.detail: The revised T2 bullet still says T2 is “the default for every operator act in family A, and for family B with `require_approval = false` until switched on,” while §4.3 says Class B `require_approval` defaults to **false** and both `--yes --reason` and `--approval A` are accepted. Since T2 means per-instance approval and `require_approval = false` means no approval is required, an implementation following the literal T2 default would treat family B verbs such as `upgrade --self` as gated and refuse `upgrade --self --yes --reason`, exactly the behavior the fix was meant to remove. The document should state the effective default for family B is disabled, not list T2 as the default while `require_approval` is false.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §7 T2 bullet vs §4.3

chunk_findings.detail: The prior LOW finding is not fully fixed: the revised text still defines `wait_s` as a mode that "lets one elicitation prompt be answered inside the same call when the client supports it." That is a bounded hold of up to 45 s while waiting for an operator. Example: an agent calls `ddflow_session ask wait_s=45` under a client that supports elicitation; if the operator does not answer until the timeout, the tool call blocks the agent for ~45 s, which is exactly the hold `[r-lock-cycle-selfheal]` prohibits. The new wording only says it is "never polling or holding a lease"; it does not remove the hold while waiting, and the rule prohibits hold while waiting, lease or not.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §10 `ddflow_session ask ... wait_s`

With no signer configured, a T3 act “can be answered at L1 only to enroll the first signer.” But D-RA-3 and this same doc state a same-uid agent can forge L1 by editing files, so an attacker can forge an L1 terminal answer and enroll its own signer key while no signer exists. From then on it controls the signer and can produce the L4 signatures required for every later T3 act. The new `doctor` warning does not block this, and §4.2’s assertion that L4 is “a signature the agent cannot make” is false along this path. The original high-severity issue remains.

chunk_findings.detail: This delta does not modify §10. The proposal still adds `ddflow_session ask` with `wait_s`, which blocks on elicitation while the caller waits for operator approval or a timeout. That is a direct hold while waiting and violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting. The triage claimed this was fixed in commit d3e7bb16b, but the shown diff leaves the blocking hold in place, so the finding still holds.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §10 `ddflow_session ask ... wait_s`

chunk_findings.detail: The revised T2 bullet still says T2 is “the default for every operator act in family A, and for family B with `require_approval = false` until switched on,” while §4.3 says Class B `require_approval` defaults to **false** and both `--yes --reason` and `--approval A` are accepted. Since T2 means per-instance approval and `require_approval = false` means no approval is required, an implementation following the literal T2 default would treat family B verbs such as `upgrade --self` as gated and refuse `upgrade --self --yes --reason`, exactly the behavior the fix was meant to remove. The document should state the effective default for family B is disabled, not list T2 as the default while `require_approval` is false.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §7 T2 bullet vs §4.3

chunk_findings.detail: The prior LOW finding is not fully fixed: the revised text still defines `wait_s` as a mode that "lets one elicitation prompt be answered inside the same call when the client supports it." That is a bounded hold of up to 45 s while waiting for an operator. Example: an agent calls `ddflow_session ask wait_s=45` under a client that supports elicitation; if the operator does not answer until the timeout, the tool call blocks the agent for ~45 s, which is exactly the hold `[r-lock-cycle-selfheal]` prohibits. The new wording only says it is "never polling or holding a lease"; it does not remove the hold while waiting, and the rule prohibits hold while waiting, lease or not.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §10 `ddflow_session ask ... wait_s`

chunk_findings.detail: The revised Q6 still leaves the empty-signer bootstrap compromise open. Q4 in the same table says `[approvals].signers` is read from the commit allowed-signers file when unset, and D-RA-3 records that a same-uid agent can edit files. On a fresh install with no signer, a malicious same-uid agent can write its own public key into that file as the "user or company layer" enrollment path before any operator enrolls a real signer. The replacement text does not require this first enrollment itself to be signed by a pre-existing trusted key or handled by a separate uid/remote store, so the attacker's key becomes the trusted first signer, and every later "T3 signed only" action can be authorized by that attacker's L4 signature. Removing the L1 terminal exception from the approval path does not answer finding 5; it moves the unprotected root-of-trust write outside the approval path without securing the signer file itself.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md Q6 row

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten `ask` action is described as returning a handle “at once, never blocking,” but the same sentence retains a blocking fallback: if `RA-probe-harness` decides an elicitation prompt cannot be issued without an open tool call and the operator has opted into `[approvals].elicit_wait_s` (up to the 45 s run-handle limit), the call can still hold the tool call while waiting for the operator to answer or time out. Concrete example: `elicit_wait_s=45` is set, the client cannot prompt out-of-band, and the operator does not answer promptly; an agent calling `ddflow_session ask` then blocks for ~45 s inside the tool call instead of taking the next item, violating [r-lock-cycle-selfheal]’s “agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting.” The prior LOW is therefore not fully fixed despite the “ask never blocks” triage.

chunk_findings.detail: The recommended default in Q6 allows T3 actions (approval config, roles, signers, forbidden-commands, key rotation) to be satisfied by L1 terminal "when no signer is configured". However, D-RA-3 explicitly states that a same-uid agent can forge L1-L3 by editing files. With no signer configured, a malicious or compromised same-uid agent can forge an L1 terminal approval and execute any T3 action, e.g., add an attacker-controlled signer or rotate keys, permanently compromising the approval system. This bootstrap hole makes the proposed default unsafe and defeats the control the design is intended to provide.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md Q6 (and D-RA-3)

chunk_findings.detail: The design is internally contradictory about Class B relayed consent. §4.3 says the old `--yes --reason` flags “keep working until a tier says otherwise (section 7),” but §7 makes T2 per-instance approval “the default for every operator act in family A and B,” including `upgrade --self`, `plan confirm`, and skew override. Under the document’s own default, the tier does say otherwise immediately. If §7 is implemented as written, an `upgrade --self --yes --reason` call must be refused, so §4.3’s compatibility statement is false. If §4.3 is taken as true and those flags remain accepted by default, a prompt-injected instruction can make the agent self-authorize with an invented reason, contradicting the stated goal of “no forgery by classes 1 and 2, by construction.”
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §4.3 vs §7

chunk_findings.detail: The proposal adds `ddflow_session ask` with `wait_s`, which “blocks on elicitation when the client supports it.” This is a direct hold while waiting for operator approval and violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal], which states agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting. Example: an agent invoking this action blocks inside the tool call until the operator answers or a timeout fires, creating the exact stall the rule forbids.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §10 `ddflow_session ask ... wait_s`

chunk_findings.detail: §4.2 claims that carrying proof and re-verifying it in `verdict` “closes Finding 1 for levels L2 and above.” But §5 defines L2 harness attestation as verified only “as far as the client’s integrity” and its own channel table says a same-uid agent can forge L2 by an auto-accept hook or by editing the hook/transcript record. In that environment the agent can produce a passing L2 proof and append the corresponding `ask.answered` line; re-verifying that forged proof still succeeds, so Finding 1 is not closed for L2. The closure claim requires an unreachable writer/client, which the proposal neither requires nor verifies.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/research/remote-approvals.md §4.2 vs §5

chunk_findings.detail: The revised Q6 still leaves the bootstrap compromise from the prior finding intact. D-RA-3 establishes that a same-uid agent can forge L1-L3 by editing files. Once a signer exists, later T3 actions require L4, but the attacker now controls the signing key and can sign arbitrary T3 requests (rotation, roles, forbidden-commands). The doctor flag "T3 protected only by L1 until done" is post hoc and does not block the enrollment or later signed actions, so the same compromise remains; the new wording only narrows the escape hatch to the one forgeable action that is sufficient to bootstrap trust.

chunk_findings.detail: The Q6/Q4 edit still does not close the prior bootstrap takeovers: it anchors the signer list in a digest pin stored "in the user layer (outside the repo)," but D-RA-3 in this same decision records that a malicious or compromised same-uid agent can forge L1-L3 by editing files, and a user-layer pin file is exactly that kind of agent-editable file. On a fresh install with no signer pinned, the agent writes an attacker-controlled SSH/FIDO2 public key list and writes the matching digest into the user-layer pin file; a digest is not a signature and requires no operator secret, so the agent can produce both. `doctor` then sees a pinned signer, and an L4 approval signed by the attacker's private key passes verification, allowing arbitrary T3 acts such as key rotation or signer changes. The rationale that "the residual risk before enrollment equals today's" is false because the agent can mint the entire root of trust.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md Q6 row (with Q4 row)

chunk_findings.detail: The new rule pins a digest of the signer list out-of-band and says `[approvals].signers` and the allowed-signers fallback are honoured **only when they match that pin**, with an edited signer file ignored. The same paragraph then says key rotation is a T3 act signed by a key already in the pinned list. A rotation necessarily changes the signer list, so after a signed rotation the new `[approvals].signers` file no longer matches the existing pin and, by the clause just stated, is ignored. Example: pinned signers are {A,B}; A is compromised, and B signs a T3 rotation to {B,C}. The resulting signer file has digest ≠ pin({A,B}), so it is ignored and compromised key A remains honored. Because the pin lives in a layer the agent cannot write, the T3 act cannot update the pin, and the diff does not describe an out-of-band pin update as part of rotation; therefore the documented rotation cannot take effect, leaving a compromised signer unremovable.

chunk_findings.detail: D-RA-2 states a relayed “the operator agreed” never satisfies a gated command, but the Q2 recommended default says to keep accepting `--yes --reason` for `upgrade`, `plan confirm`, and skew override for one release. Concrete input: an agent runs `upgrade --self --yes --reason "operator said yes in chat"` during that release; an implementation following Q2 accepts the relayed consent and performs the gated act, directly contradicting D-RA-2 (and Q6, which sets T2 minimum level to L1). The document’s own proposed defaults are therefore internally inconsistent and instruct contrary implementations.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md D-RA-2 and Q2 row

chunk_findings.detail: D-RA-1 asserts absolutely that “The agent identity still cannot answer,” but D-RA-3 says that without a separate uid, signature, or remote store, a same-uid agent can forge L1-L3 by editing files. On a single-uid host, the same OS user the agent runs as can edit the ask/transcript record or execute the documented L1 CLI (`ddflow approvals approve`), which D-RA-3 says is forgeable, so the agent can in fact answer an L1/L2 request; D-RA-1’s unqualified prohibition is false in the environment the document itself flags.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/remote-approvals.md D-RA-1 and D-RA-3

chunk_findings.detail: The previous bootstrap finding is not fixed by adding “visible and costlier to forge, not unforgeable.” Q4/Q6 still recommend a user-layer digest pin on hosts with no root-owned/company-pack/signed-commit store, and D-RA-3 says a same-uid agent can edit user-layer files. Concrete scenario: on a fresh single-uid host, a malicious same-uid agent writes an attacker-controlled signer list and its matching digest pin before enrollment (or overwrites the operator’s pin later), suppressing the doctor “no approval signer pinned” warning; Q6’s T3=L4 verification then trusts that attacker key, allowing the agent to sign T3 signer enrollment/rotation/config acts and take over the approval system. Stating the limit does not remove the path.
